# Measuring Size-Specialized Malloc with GOEXPERIMENT

## Thesis

Go **1.27** already documents size-specialized `mallocgc` for known sizes ≤80 bytes. This chapter is the **measurement** companion: the same microbenchmarks with the default build versus `GOEXPERIMENT=nosizespecializedmalloc`, so you can see the win on your CPU instead of trusting the blog's "up to ~30%" alone. The neighbouring chapter maps size classes; here we only time them.

## Mental model

```text
  compiler knows size ≤ 80B
        │
        ├─ default 1.27 → call mallocgcSmall…SCn directly
        └─ GOEXPERIMENT=nosizespecializedmalloc → generic mallocgc path
```

Opt-out is a bisect tool. The Go team expects the experiment knob to go away in **1.28**.

## Worked examples

Verified with **Go 1.27.2** linux/amd64 on an Intel Xeon guest.

### Case 1: tiny struct vs 80B vs 96B slices

```go
// main_test.go
package main

import "testing"

type tiny struct{ a, b, c, d int64 } // 32 bytes

func BenchmarkTinyAlloc(b *testing.B) {
	b.ReportAllocs()
	var sink *tiny
	for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
		sink = &tiny{1, 2, 3, 4}
	}
	_ = sink
}

func BenchmarkSlice80(b *testing.B) {
	b.ReportAllocs()
	var sink []byte
	for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
		sink = make([]byte, 80)
	}
	_ = sink
}

func BenchmarkSlice96(b *testing.B) {
	b.ReportAllocs()
	var sink []byte
	for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
		sink = make([]byte, 96)
	}
	_ = sink
}
```

```bash
go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5
GOEXPERIMENT=nosizespecializedmalloc go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5
```

Representative lines from this run (5 counts each; lower ns/op is better):

| Benchmark | Default (ns/op) | nosizespecialized (ns/op) |
|-----------|-----------------|---------------------------|
| TinyAlloc (32 B) | ~12.6–13.8 | ~17.6–18.4 |
| Slice80 | ~25–27 | ~28–33 |
| Slice96 (above 80) | ~30–34 | ~31–32 |

The **32-byte** path shows the clearest gap (~30% here). **96 bytes** sits outside the specialized window and barely moves — a useful control.

## Trap

**Declaring victory from one microbenchmark.** Size specialization is a small overall win (~1% on alloc-heavy programs per the release notes). If your profile is dominated by large buffers or stack allocation, you will see noise, not a rewrite-worthy speedup.

## Boring rule

Stay on Go 1.27+ and let the compiler specialize. Reach for `GOEXPERIMENT=nosizespecializedmalloc` only when bisecting a suspected allocator regression, then file an issue if you need the knob to stay.

## Try this

1. Add a `BenchmarkMakeN` where `n` is a runtime variable and compare.
2. Run with `-benchtime=2s` on a quiet machine and compute medians.
3. Cross-check against `go tool pprof` alloc profiles on a real service.
